The database for studies on long-term, short-term, and reproductive toxicity is insufficient, limiting the ability to fully assess the risks. 3. A teratology study in rabbits identified a systemic NOAEL (No Observed Adverse Effect Level) of 5 mg/kg body weight per day, which is lower than the LOAELs (Lowest Observed Adverse Effect Levels) and NOAELs reported in other studies. 4. This NOAEL was selected for deriving a TDI (Tolerable Daily Intake). 5. Methyl parathion (CAS No. 298-00-0) is a non-systemic insecticide and acaricide widely used on crops, particularly cotton. 6. In the environment, methyl parathion primarily partitions to air and soil, with minimal movement through soil, and neither the parent compound nor its breakdown products are expected to reach groundwater. 7. Microbial degradation is the primary route for environmental breakdown of methyl parathion, with half-lives in water ranging from weeks to months. 8. The general population may be exposed to methyl parathion through air, water, or food. 9. A dose of 12.3 mg/kg body weight per day was derived from human studies based on the depression of erythrocyte and plasma cholinesterase activities. 10. Long-term studies in mice and rats showed that methyl parathion decreased cholinesterase activity but did not induce carcinogenic effects. 11. Methyl parathion was mutagenic in bacteria, but no evidence of genotoxicity was found in mammalian systems. 12. A 2-year study in rats identified adverse effects such as retinal degeneration, sciatic nerve demyelination, reduced body weight, anemia, and decreased brain acetylcholinesterase activity at 25 mg/kg body weight per day. 13. An uncertainty factor of 100 was applied to account for interspecies and intraspecies variability. 14. Toxicological endpoints observed in experimental animals, other than acetylcholinesterase inhibition, were considered more appropriate for risk assessment than human NOAELs for cholinesterase inhibition. 15. Methyl parathion intake from all sources is generally low and well below the upper limit of the ADI (Acceptable Daily Intake). 16. The health-based value for methyl parathion is significantly higher than concentrations likely to be found in drinking water, making it unlikely to pose a hazard under normal conditions. 17. Therefore, establishing a formal guideline value for methyl parathion in drinking water is not deemed necessary. 18. Methyl tertiary-butyl ether (MTBE) is primarily used as a gasoline additive. 19. Surface water contamination by MTBE can occur due to gasoline spills, but its high volatility leads to significant evaporation. 20. Groundwater contamination from spills and leaking storage tanks is more persistent and problematic. 21. MTBE is not genotoxic, as evidenced by numerous in vitro and in vivo studies in mammalian and non-mammalian systems, which mostly produced negative results. 22. MTBE is considered a rodent carcinogen, but its carcinogenic response occurs only at high exposure levels that also induce other adverse effects. 23. The available data are inconclusive for human carcinogenic risk assessment, and no health-based guideline value has been derived for MTBE. 24. Metolachlor (CAS No. 51218-45-2) is a selective pre-emergence herbicide used on various crops. 25. Metolachlor can be lost from soil through biodegradation, photodegradation, and volatilization, and it is fairly mobile, potentially contaminating groundwater under certain conditions, though it is mostly found in surface water. 26. A 1-year study in dogs showed decreased kidney weight at the two highest dose levels. 27. In 2-year rodent studies, toxicological effects included decreased body weight gain and survival in female mice at the highest dose level, while rats showed decreased body weight gain and food consumption. 28. There is no evidence that metolachlor is carcinogenic in mice, though liver tumors in female rats and nasal tumors in male rats have been observed. 29. Metolachlor is not genotoxic. 30. Microcystins (MCs) are naturally occurring heptapeptides produced by cyanobacteria, primarily in freshwater environments. 31. Among the over 250 identified MCs, only a few occur frequently and in high concentrations, with microcystin-LR (MC-LR) being the most common and extensively studied. 32. Drinking water is the most likely route of exposure to MCs, especially when surface water with cyanobacterial blooms is used as a source. 33. Recreational activities in lakes with cyanobacterial blooms may also lead to intermittent exposure to high concentrations of MCs. 34. Limited data suggest that MCs may accumulate in some food items. 35. Acute effects of MC poisoning include intrahepatic hemorrhage, while chronic effects include reduced efficacy of proliferation control mechanisms in tumor cells. 36. Cases of liver damage and fatalities have been reported from exposure to MCs in inadequately treated drinking water and renal dialysis using contaminated water. 37. In 2006, the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) classified MC-LR as a possible human carcinogen (Group 2B) based on evidence for tumor promotion. 38. The provisional guideline values for MCs are based on a study in mice using MC-LR, corroborated by a similar study in rats, with the liver identified as the most sensitive organ. 39. Recent research suggesting effects on reproductive organs from prolonged low-concentration exposure requires further corroboration due to methodological and reporting deficiencies. 40. Effective control of cyanobacterial blooms includes catchment and source water management, such as reducing nutrient loading and altering reservoir stratification and mixing. 41. Filtration methods, such as soil, slow sand, or riverbank filtration, are effective for removing intact cyanobacterial cells and cell-bound MCs. 42. Oxidation with chlorine or ozone, as well as granular activated carbon (GAC) and some powdered activated carbon (PAC) applications, are effective for removing dissolved MCs. 43. Chlorination and ozonation at sufficiently high doses and contact times degrade dissolved MCs, though elevated organic carbon in bloom situations increases disinfectant demand. 44. Monitoring and optimizing treatment processes are essential to target the removal of both cells and dissolved toxins.
